title: Token Bridges run a 2-of-2 validator quorum while Governance Bridges run 4-of-7, tuning security to payload
content:
Every bridge in this chunk configures its two components differently and identically across chains. The Token Bridge validators are "LayerZero and Nethermind" with a quorum of 2/2 (A.4.2.2.2.3.3.1.1–2, A.4.2.2.3.3.3.1.1–2, A.4.2.2.4.3.3.1.1–2). The Governance Bridge runs seven validators — LayerZero, Nethermind, Canary, Deutsche Telekom, P2P, Horizen, Luganodes — at 4/7 (A.4.2.2.2.3.3.2.1–2, A.4.2.2.3.3.3.2.1–2, A.4.2.2.4.3.3.2.1–2).

The two configurations sit at opposite ends of the safety/liveness trade. A 2/2 quorum is maximal safety: forging an asset transfer requires compromising *both* validators, and either validator can unilaterally stop token flow by declining to attest. Sky accepts that fragility for money movement — a stalled bridge is an inconvenience, a forged mint is a loss.

A 4/7 quorum inverts the priority. Governance messages must be deliverable even when validators are down or unwilling, because the Governance Bridge is the channel through which Sky exercises control on the remote chain — including, plausibly, responses to trouble. Three simultaneous failures are tolerated, and no single validator can block a governance action.

The reason both can coexist is the Token/Governance split. Nothing forces one quorum policy on both payload types, so each gets the policy its failure modes deserve: veto-friendly for value, censorship-resistant for control.

A residual dependency is worth naming: LayerZero appears in both sets on every chain, so a LayerZero-level failure degrades token bridging everywhere (it cannot be replaced without breaking 2/2) even though governance messaging would survive it.
description: Identical across Solana, Avalanche and Plasma: asset transfers require unanimity of two validators so either can veto, while governance messages tolerate three faulty validators out of seven.
